origin_region: Valle del Cauca · La Cumbre · Bitaco
cultivar: Seed-grown and clonal bushes, reportedly of Indian and Sri Lankan origin, planted from the mid-twentieth century onwards
processing: Orthodox and CTC black tea from a single high-altitude estate: hand-picked leaf withered, rolled or cut, fully oxidised and fired; the estate also makes green and a little white tea, and most of its output goes into the owner's domestic tea-bag brand.
harvest_season: Plucked all year on the equator, on a cycle of a few weeks; the drier months (roughly December to March and July to August) give the brightest leaf, but there are no seasonal grades.
appearance_dry: Dark, wiry, twisted leaves with a few golden tips in the specialty grade; small granular leaf in the tea-bag grade.
taste_profile: Mild, soft and lightly floral with a gentle malt, a honeyed sweetness and low tannin; a clean, easy high-grown black tea that sits between a light Ceylon and a Darjeeling second flush in weight.

brewing.notes: Western style, three minutes, no milk needed; the whole-leaf specialty grade can be steeped shorter and resteeped once or twice.

vintage_note: Sold year-round under the estate's domestic brand (Hindú) in tea bags across Colombia, and as 'Bitaco' specialty loose leaf in small packs from the estate and a few export partners; neither is dated by harvest, since the equatorial estate picks continuously. Buy the loose specialty grade and use it within a year or two.
description:
Colombia is coffee country, and its one tea estate is a curiosity most Colombians have never heard of, even though many of them drink its tea. Bitaco is a plantation in the cloud forest above La Cumbre in Valle del Cauca, at around 1,800 to 2,000 metres, owned by Agrícola Himalaya, the company behind the Hindú tea-bag brand that sits on supermarket shelves across the country. The gardens were planted around the middle of the twentieth century, reportedly with Indian and Sri Lankan material, and have been expanded and modernised since.

The estate picks by hand all year, as the equatorial climate allows, and makes orthodox and CTC black tea, plus green and a little white tea, in its own factory. Most of the volume goes into the domestic tea bags; a smaller specialty line, sold under the Bitaco name, is where the whole-leaf teas end up, and it is this line that has reached specialty shops abroad over the last decade.

The black tea is high-grown and tastes it: mild, soft and lightly floral, with gentle malt, honeyed sweetness and low tannin, nearer to a light Ceylon or a Darjeeling second flush than to anything heavy. It is clean and easy, brews well Western-style without milk, and the whole-leaf grade takes a second steep. It is not a tea of great depth, but it is a well-made one from a place nobody expects.

In Colombia you will meet it as Hindú tea bags; the thing to buy is the Bitaco loose leaf, from the estate's shop, Colombian specialty retailers or the few importers who carry it. There are no fakes and no vintages, only the choice between the bag grade and the specialty grade.

If you collect single-estate teas from unexpected places, Bitaco belongs on the shelf beside Gorreana from the Azores and Charleston from South Carolina; and the natural comparison in the cup is a mid-grown Ceylon.
sources_note: No Wikipedia article for Bitaco or Colombian tea was found; 'Black tea' is used as the generic umbrella. Planting decade (1960s), altitude and the origin of the plant material are from the estate's own history and press coverage and should be checked. Ecuador's small tea industry (Sangay) was considered and omitted for lack of confidence.
